Why this exists

The presets split in two, and only half were worth keeping. This month, Last month and Custom range are single-cycle questions the stepper answers better. Last 30 days, Last 90 days and Year to date are trend questions — and D3 already requires the trend charts to carry their own window. Making that window selectable costs one control and closes the gap.

It is a chart control, not a date range. Placed on the chart card, never in the header, so it cannot be mistaken for the page scope. Stat cards, transaction table and category breakdown stay on the stepper's cycle — the constraint D3 exists to protect.

Both ranges are always named. Two time windows on one page is only confusing if either is implicit. The stepper states its cycle; the chart subtitle states its range and its bucket size.

Bucket size adapts. 30 days daily, 90 days weekly, YTD and 12 months monthly. The old presets kept monthly bars at every range, so Last 30 days rendered as one bar — the reason the preset was weak, not just the control.

Scope boundary — do not cross The lookback must not be persisted as a user preference that outlives the session, must not appear in the header, and must not be readable by the stat cards. Any of the three turns it back into the page-level date range D3 removed.

What this changes

Windowing is a requirement, not an optimisation. At ~2,000 rows per account and 4–8 accounts, Activity and Account detail must render a window (60 rows desktop, 30 mobile) and load on scroll. Today both render the full filtered set.

The result bar earns its keep. Count, sum and sort pinned above the rows — the only way to know a filter did what you meant without scrolling to the end.

Month jump replaces paging. 24 months of history is 24 stepper clicks. The rail jumps and carries each month's net; on mobile it's a bottom-bar action.

Above 12 categories, drop the pie. 20–50 categories makes a pie unreadable and its legend taller than the chart. Ranked bars, with a tail row that opens.

Search needs counts and groups. A common term matches hundreds of rows. Group by kind, cap each group at three, state the real count, and hand off to Activity.

Import problems group by cause. 37 problems in 1,284 rows is five causes. Fix the cause, clear the rows; errors block, warnings don't.

Ceilings to design against Transactions 2,000 per account · accounts 4–8 · categories 20–50. Budgets & Goals and Split transaction stay inside their current layouts at these numbers — no dense variant needed.

What these decisions cost, and what they need

D1 · the setting is two radios, not a toggle. A toggle needs one label that reads correctly in both states, and on a financial setting "Carry overspend: off" is the kind of double negative people misread. Each option shows the figure it produces — $600.00 or $457.70 — so the choice is made on numbers rather than on wording.

D1 · the word "rollover" is retired for the deficit. The existing per-budget toggle keeps it, for surplus, which is what most people already think it means. The deficit question becomes "When you overspend" — the two controls now describe different things in different words, instead of one checkbox silently doing both.

D1b · Overspending is not a warning strip. Under 'reset' it is the only record that the overspend happened, so it needs to be a first-class report — per category, with the consecutive-cycle count, which is the figure that distinguishes one bad month from a budget that is simply set too low. Three consecutive cycles over on Dining is a budget problem, not a spending problem.

D1b · it names the active setting. Both the report and the budget form say which behaviour is live and link to change it. Without that, a user seeing $142.30 over cannot tell whether next month is already reduced.

D3 · the trend chart keeps its own window. The stepper moves the 12-month lookback rather than narrowing it — a bar chart scoped to one cycle is one bar. The chart labels its range (12 months to Sep 2026) and outlines the selected cycle, so the relationship between stepper and chart is visible rather than inferred.

D3 · this removes ~240px of chrome. The seven presets and the two bordered control cards (9a annotations 2 and 3) all go. The stepper was already in row two for every other screen, so Reports stops being the exception and the first figure appears higher up the page.

D4 · nothing new to draw. 12a already covers the card-payment flow at all three sizes, and add-transaction-spec.md §1.3 covers the kind. The only addition is that the Liabilities group in 5a is now confirmed rather than proposed.

Open question worth your call. Under 'carry', should the carried deficit be capped so a budget can't go negative? A $900 spend on a $600 budget would open October at −$300.00, which is a budget you cannot meet without spending nothing. Clamping at zero is the safer default; I have not assumed it.

The rule this frame is showing

Seven tabs are one tab stop, not seven

A roving tabIndex: the active tab is 0, the rest are -1, and ←/→ move the selection. Tab then leaves the group. Without this, replacing the rail with seven tabs costs a keyboard user six extra stops before the content on every screen.

The active tab announces itself

aria-current="page" on the active destination. There are zero occurrences of aria-current in the codebase today — Sidebar and BottomNav mark the active item with a background tint alone, so a screen reader cannot tell which of the destinations you are on.

Nine stops to content without the skip link; two with it. The numbers are the tab order, not a visual treatment.

Duration tokens — replacing eleven ad-hoc values
TokenValueReplaces
--dur-instant 100ms .press-scale · duration-100 on dialog, dropdown, popover, select
--dur-fast 160ms .reorder-motion 160ms · .reorder-handle 140ms · duration-150 on the sheet backdrop and Reports chips
--dur-base 200ms .hover-lift · duration-200 on BottomNav, Sidebar, sheet content, Login, the pie card
--dur-enter 280ms .animate-scale-in 0.28s · .animate-page-in 0.32s
--dur-sheet 260ms .m3-bottom-sheet — already correct, and the one duration with a considered curve
--dur-meter 500ms duration-500 on progress fills — BudgetsPage:871, ReportsPage:1059, :1305. Deliberate and worth keeping
One easing curve already exists — name it

All four keyframe utilities use cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) consistently. That is genuinely good work; it just isn't a variable, so every new transition written in Tailwind gets ease instead. --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) and the existing curve becomes the default rather than an exception.

Reduced motion — what the block covers, and what it misses
Covered
.animate-page-in .animate-fade-up .animate-scale-in .reorder-motion .press-scale:active .hover-lift:hover .m3-bottom-sheet

Two separate @media (prefers-reduced-motion) blocks — one beside the sheet rule, one at the end of the file. Worth merging.

Not covered
animate-pulse — every skeleton (25a) animate-spin — 5 spinners animate-in / animate-out — dialog, sheet, dropdown, popover, tooltip, select zoom-in-95 / zoom-out-95 slide-in-from-* — every popover side transition-colors — ~40 sites transition-transform — chevrons, switch thumb

The block names four utility classes, so everything from tw-animate-css and every Tailwind transition still animates. A blanket rule for * inside the query, with the colour transitions allowed back, covers the rest.

Order on mobile

Header, then content, then the FAB, then the bottom nav — DOM order, so no tabIndex above 0 anywhere. The FAB is visually last but must come before the nav in the DOM, or Tab lands on Home before the primary action on the page.

3Content — the cards above
4Add transaction (FAB)
5Bottom nav — one stop, arrows within
Sheets and modals

On open, focus moves to the sheet's first heading, not its first field — so the title is announced before the form. On close, focus returns to the control that opened it. Neither is specified today; the primitives trap focus but say nothing about restore.

Five stops to cross a mobile screen. No skip link needed at this size — the header is two controls.

What changed, and why

1. aria-current does not appear in the codebase. Zero occurrences. Sidebar.tsx and BottomNav.tsx both mark the active destination with a background tint and colour only, so a screen-reader user cannot tell which of the destinations they are on. This matters more under 2B, which puts seven tabs where the rail was.

2. Seven tabs must be one tab stop. A roving tabIndex — active tab 0, others -1, arrows to move — plus role="tablist". Without it the nav change costs six extra stops before content on every screen, which would make 2B measurably worse than the rail it replaces.

3. Four clickable rows are focusable but not operable. DashboardCategoryPieCard:29, BudgetsPage:1090, TransactionsPage:481 and TransactionRow:177 all set tabIndex={0} with no onKeyDown — you can Tab to them and Enter does nothing. Only DashboardTransactionRow:23 handles Enter and Space, and it hand-rolls the handler. One button-based row component fixes all five.

4. Reduced motion covers four class names. The block lists .animate-page-in, .animate-fade-up, .animate-scale-in and .reorder-motion — so every tw-animate-css utility still runs: animate-pulse on all skeletons, animate-spin on five spinners, and the animate-in/zoom/slide-in-from-* set on dialog, sheet, dropdown, popover, tooltip and select. It reads as complete and is not.

5. Eleven durations, no token. 100 / 140 / 150 / 160 / 180 / 200 / 260 / 280 / 320 / 420 / 500ms across the CSS and Tailwind classes. Six tokens cover all of them, and only --dur-meter (500ms, progress fills) and --dur-sheet (260ms) are deliberate enough to keep as-is.

6. The easing curve is right and unnamed. cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) is used consistently across all four keyframes — good work. It just isn't a variable, so anything written in Tailwind silently gets ease instead.

7. Two ring widths. The ui/ primitives use focus-visible:ring-3; the hand-rolled rows use ring-2. Pick one — the primitives' is correct and already everywhere.

8. No skip link. Nine stops from page load to content at 1920 under 2B. One <a href="#main">, visible on focus, is the whole fix.

9. Focus restore is unspecified. The primitives trap focus inside a modal, but nothing says where focus goes on open (the heading, not the first field) or on close (back to the trigger). With 5a's menu opening a form, and 5b's picker preceding one, this is a real sequence to get right.

10. Stagger reaches 480ms. .anim-delay-8 on .animate-fade-up means the eighth card starts arriving half a second after the first, on top of a 420ms animation. Cap the stagger at four steps and let the rest arrive together.

September August July

Built on a message that already exists and is good — useBudgets.ts:45, "Budgets for this cycle are not cached. Reconnect to load them." It just has no surface, so it renders as a bare red line. Here it gets an action and names what is available.

What changed, and why

1. A failed fetch is indistinguishable from an empty account. The serious one. useTransactions.ts:87, useAccounts.ts:38, useCategories.ts:36, useSavingsGoals.ts:40 and useLoanPurchases.ts:53 all set an error string on a failed read — and the pages that consume them render their empty state instead. So a connection failure shows "No transactions found" and invites you to create one. Compounds the empty-vs-filtered confusion in 20a.

2. Raw Postgres messages are the user-facing copy. Roughly twenty call sites return or set error.message straight from Supabase — useAccounts (5), useLoanPurchases (5), useExchangeRates (3), useBudgets (2), useCategories, useSubcategories, useTransactions, useSavingsGoals, SettingsPage:274. A unique-constraint violation reads as duplicate key value violates unique constraint "categories_user_id_name_key". Map the handful of codes that actually occur — unique violation, RLS denial, connection failure — to sentences, and keep the raw text collapsed for support.

3. There is no notification surface. ui/undo-toast.tsx is the only thing resembling one and it's used by two pages for undo-delete. Every other outcome — success, failure, partial failure — is an inline <p>, or nothing. Three severities on one surface covers the app.

4. Three errors go to the console only. AuthContext.tsx:40 profile fetch, :55 getSession, :87 sign-out. The third matters most: a failed sign-out is silent, so the user believes they've signed out on a device where they haven't.

5. Partial failure already exists and deserves a pattern. AccountTransactionsPage.tsx:536 is honest and well-written — "Payment transfer was recorded, but saving the payment record failed… Statement tracking may be out of date." It's the only one, and it's inline on one page. Two-phase writes elsewhere need the same treatment.

6. The error boundary says four words. ui/error-boundary.tsx:32 renders "Something went wrong." with no retry and no reload. Scope it to the section that failed, say what's still safe, and offer recovery.

7. role="alert" appears in one file. LoanPurchaseTracker uses it on four messages; the twenty-odd other inline errors don't, so screen readers never announce them. Mechanical fix, and it belongs in whatever component replaces the inline <p>.

8. A negative-margin hack, nine times. className="text-sm text-destructive px-1 -mt-2" is repeated verbatim across BudgetsPage (4), AccountTransactionsPage (3) and CategoriesPage (2) — pulling the error up into the gap above it. One <FormError> with its own spacing removes all nine.

9. Off-system colours in budget bars. BudgetsPage.tsx:641 uses bg-yellow-500 and bg-emerald-500 raw, where the app has GOLD and INCOME. Same class as the Home reminder strips (Part 1 #24).

What changed, and why

1. Four places hand-roll the pulse. ReportsPage.tsx lines 948, 1186 and 1236 use <div className="h-full w-full rounded-lg bg-muted animate-pulse" /> and line 1285 uses h-8 rounded-lg bg-muted animate-pulse — reimplementing <Skeleton> inline while the same file imports it on line 40 and uses it correctly six other times. Same drift as EmptyState.

2. One component, five radii. Skeleton bakes in rounded-md, then call sites override it with rounded-xl, rounded-2xl, rounded-[20px], rounded-lg and plain rounded. Cards in this app are 20px; a skeleton at rounded-md standing in for one is the wrong shape. Either the default matches the card radius or every call site passes it — not both.

3. Skeletons don't describe what they replace. Heights are a loose scale — h-8, h-10, h-11, h-12, h-14, h-16, h-20, h-24, h-36, h-40, h-48, h-56, h-64, h-[150px] — and each is one flat block. A structured skeleton keeps the row grid, icon tile and dividers real and greys only the text runs, so the layout doesn't shift when data lands.

4. Loading and refetching are different states. Stepping the month cycle currently swaps the list for skeletons even though you already have data on screen. Keeping the previous cycle visible at reduced opacity with a progress rule and a named target ("Loading August…") is faster to read and doesn't lose your scroll position.

5. The shell never loads. Nav, period stepper, page title and the primary action depend on no query, so they should be live and interactive from the first frame — including the ability to step away from a cycle that's still loading.

6. Two spinner treatments coexist. Loader2 with animate-spin appears in ImportCSVDialog and TransactionForm; everything else pulses. Spinner for an action you triggered, skeleton for content arriving — worth stating as a rule rather than leaving to the call site.

Data deletion

How to delete your data

You can permanently remove everything Ledger holds about you from inside the app — no email request, no waiting period. This page lists exactly what we store and how to erase it.

Last updated May 2, 2026 4 minute read

What we hold about you

Your name, email address and profile picture, received from Google at sign-in
Every financial account you created in Ledger
All transactions, categories and budgets you entered
Your preferences — default currency, colour scheme, dashboard layout
Session tokens that keep you signed in

How to delete it

01 Sign in to LedgerOpen the app and sign in with your Google account.
02 Open SettingsClick the Settings icon in the header, or press ⌘K and search for it.
03 Choose Delete my accountIt's the last item in the Account section. A confirmation dialog opens.
04 Type DELETE to confirmType DELETE in the field and choose Delete forever.

There is no grace period

The moment you confirm, your profile, accounts, transactions, categories and budgets are erased in a single operation. Nothing is recoverable.

What changed, and why

1. One layout, three documents. Privacy, Terms and Data deletion each rebuild the same skeleton — back links, icon, title, last-updated line, sections, separators, footer — in their own file. A single <LegalPage> taking a title, a date and section content removes three copies of the same markup, and stops the three pages drifting apart.

2. Delete the atmospheric layer. DataDeletionPage opens with four absolutely-positioned decorative elements — a 700×500 radial gradient, a 3%-opacity dot grid, and two 480–500px bordered circles bleeding off-canvas — rendered before any content. They're invisible in practice and they're the first thing in the file. Legal pages should be plain.

3. Red is for the destructive step, not the whole page. Both section headings, all four step numbers and the summary box use --expense. Reserving it for step 04 and the no-grace-period warning makes the genuinely irreversible part legible instead of uniform.

4. The three pages link to each other. Data deletion links to Privacy, Privacy and Terms don't cross-link, and none of them can reach the other two consistently. A small tab row in the header covers it.

5. Offer the export before the deletion. Reports already exports CSV. Putting it beside irreversible instructions is the one genuinely useful addition to this page.

6. A contents rail at 1920. max-w-3xl centres the column and leaves the rest empty; the measure stays right for reading, and the freed space carries section links and the export card.

7. /terms has no routeMeta entry in App.tsx, while /privacy and /data-deletion do — so it falls through to the generic page title. One line.

What changed, and why

1. "Rollover unused budget" also rolls over overspend. The important one. rolloverAmount += surplus, and surplus = b.amount − periodSpent — which is negative in any month you went over. That deficit is carried forward and subtracted from next month's limit, compounding across periods. The label promises a reward and the code also delivers a penalty. Whatever the intended behaviour, the checkbox has to say it.

2. The toggle does nothing on non-monthly budgets. The entire rollover block is inside if (b.period === 'monthly'), so on any other period rollover_amount stays 0 — but the checkbox still renders, still saves rollover_enabled: true, and the budget card still shows a "Rollover" chip. Either disable it with the reason, or state the limitation.

3. Show the carried balance in the form. When editing a budget the accumulated figure is already computed and sitting in rollover_amount. Base limit → carried in → effective is the only way to understand why this period's allowance isn't the number you typed.

4. Rollover is clamped to 13 months, deliberately. The loop start is pinned to the fetched window because iterating from an older start_date would bank full surpluses for un-fetched months. Correct — but it means a two-year-old budget's carried balance silently starts 13 months ago, and nothing says so.

5. Unconvertible spend is dropped from the total. convertAmount returns null with no rate and the reducer skips it — so a budget with spend in an unrated currency reads under budget. Same omission the Accounts page warns about; here there's no warning at all.

6. The cycle is named. Budgets run on the pay cycle via getBudgetCycleRange, not the calendar month. The form asks for a period and never shows the resulting dates.

7. Goals compute what they need. Target, saved and an optional date are three inputs that imply a fourth number — the monthly contribution required — which the form doesn't derive. That's the number that makes a goal actionable.

8. Say that goals are manual. A savings goal has no account link; current_amount is a field you edit by hand. Transferring money to Emergency Fund doesn't move the goal, which is the reasonable assumption to make.

Offline & sync

Correcting my earlier note in this audit: there is an OfflineBanner, wired into AppLayout. The problem isn't that offline is invisible — it's that the banner shows a count and nothing else, while offlineQueue.ts silently drops and skips writes underneath it.
The four states, at 1920 width
Offline — 3 entries saved on this device, waiting to sync Review queue
Offline. Entries keep working; the count says how many are held locally.

Syncing. The hook knows the total — showing progress costs nothing.

The one that's wrong today. The banner reads "3 changes queued — reconnecting…", but nothing is reconnecting: you're already online and the drain either failed or hasn't fired. useNetworkStatus exports syncNow; the banner never calls it.
1 change couldn't be saved — it was edited elsewhere Resolve
No UI for this exists. drainQueue detects the conflict, skips the write and calls console.warn. Your edit is gone and you are never told.

What changed, and why

1. Conflicts are silent data loss. The serious one. drainQueue compares updated_at, and when a row changed elsewhere since you queued your edit it skips the write and logs console.warn("Conflict detected … skipping stale update"). The user made an edit, saw it applied locally, and it is discarded with no notice. That needs a UI, and it's the whole reason the queue-review screen above exists.

2. Items older than 30 days are deleted, also silently. MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS drops stale entries on drain with another console.warn. A phone left offline over a long trip loses entries it promised would sync.

3. "Reconnecting…" isn't true. When isOnline && !isSyncing && pendingCount > 0, the banner says "3 changes queued — reconnecting…". You're already connected; the drain simply isn't running. useNetworkStatus exposes syncNow and the banner never calls it — so the fix is a button, and the hook is already ready for it.

4. A queued row looks identical to a saved one. addTransaction returns { error: null, queued: true } and nothing renders that flag. The banner's count is the only clue, and it can't tell you which three.

5. Three different offline behaviours, no signalling. Transactions and the month cycle queue and replay. Loan purchases hard-refuse with a message — but only after you've filled the form. Accounts, budgets, categories and savings goals just return early, so they neither save nor complain. Disabling what can't work is more honest than failing at submit.

6. Progress instead of a count. drainQueue processes items in order and the total is known, so "Syncing 2 of 3" and a bar cost nothing over a spinner.

7. Say where the queue lives. It's localStorage under ledger_offline_queue, with receipts staged best-effort in IndexedDB. Clearing site data destroys unsynced entries — worth one line in the review sheet.

8. Banner styling is off-system. It sets background: var(--primary) with --primary-foreground when online and --expense-container/--expense when offline — indigo for "syncing" reads as a feature announcement, and 11px tracking-wide text is below the app's smallest body size. Gold for pending and red only for genuine failure matches the rest of this audit.

What changed, and why

1. The unitemized-debt reconciliation escapes the Add dialog. The most consequential one. That yellow warning renders only when purchases.length === 0, inside the create modal — so it's shown exactly once, before any purchase exists, and vanishes forever after. But getLoanAmountOwed(account) and the sum of the purchases can drift apart at any time, and the difference is debt with no schedule and no deadline. It belongs on the tracker, permanently, whenever the two disagree.

2. Deadlines aren't hidden four at a time. DEADLINES_PAGE_SIZE = 4 with prev/next buttons, every row collapsed by default (expandedDeadline starts null), inside a lg:grid-cols-2 half-column. Paging through a repayment schedule four rows at a time is the wrong interaction for a list you want to scan — a scrolling list with the next payment pinned and expanded reads in one pass.

3. The next payment gets an action. The tracker computes the exact next deadline and its per-purchase split, and offers no way to pay it — you leave, open Add Transaction, choose Loan repayment, re-pick the loan. 5b already builds that form; this is where it should be launched from, prefilled.

4. Imported-as-paid is shown in the bar, not just as a badge. A purchase with opening_installments_paid: 10 and no real repayments renders a 42% progress bar identical to one you actually paid down. Two segments separate "money Ledger recorded" from "opening figure you typed" — the difference matters when reconciling against a lender.

5. Recent Payment Splits becomes a table. Eight allocations render as name-over-date pairs with an amount — but the installment number, which is the thing that tells you which payment this was, is dropped entirely even though loanInstallments has it. Four columns fit easily at this width.

6. Milestones are marked. When the warranty's 24 months end, the monthly obligation drops from $620 to $480 — a genuinely useful fact that's currently derivable only by expanding rows one at a time and comparing.

7. Loan-level figures exist. Interest remaining, total monthly obligation and a debt-free date are all computable from data already loaded, and none of them appear anywhere. The five-cell band answers "when does this end and what is it costing me".

What changed, and why

1. EmptyState has no action prop. The component takes exactly icon, title, description — so Accounts renders "Add your first account to get started" with no button to do it. The instruction and the means to follow it are in different parts of the screen. Adding an action slot is a 3-line change that fixes every use at once.

2. Empty and filtered-empty are the same message. TransactionsPage.tsx:573 and AccountTransactionsPage.tsx:953 both render title="No transactions found" — whether you have zero transactions ever, or eighteen that your filter excluded. Those need opposite responses: create a record, versus widen the filter. Same for Reports' "No transactions in this period" and the 13th Month page's "No income transactions found for 2026".

3. There is no first run. A new user lands on Home with every widget rendering its own separate empty message and no indication of what to do first. Three ordered steps — account, a transaction, the pay cycle — is the real dependency chain: budgets need a cycle, everything needs an account.

4. Eight places skip the component entirely. DashboardRecentTransactionsCard, DashboardDetailDialogs (three messages), BudgetsPage, ReportsPage (two) and ThirteenthMonthPage all hand-roll a muted <p> instead — different padding, no icon, no action. Only three screens use EmptyState.

5. Placeholder shapes beat a blank page. Greyed dashed cards showing what Net Worth, Cash Flow and Budget Progress will look like explain the product better than copy does, and they make the empty state feel like a beginning rather than a failure.

6. Destinations that can't work yet are marked, not faded. Activity, Budgets, Categories and Reports are all dead ends before an account exists, so saying so beats letting someone tour four empty screens. A lock glyph plus a muted-but-legible label carries that — transparency doesn't, since an opacity-faded label reads as broken rather than deliberately inactive.

7. Setup is skippable. Forced onboarding in a finance app is where people bounce. The checklist stays available on Home until it's done.

What changed, and why

1. There are two account forms, and they disagree. The biggest finding. AccountForm in AccountsPage.tsx creates accounts; a separate EditAccountForm with its own accountSchema lives in AccountTransactionsPage.tsx and edits them. The edit schema has credit_limit, statement_day and due_day — but no loan_pay_period and no loan_due_days. You can create a loan with a repayment schedule and then never change it from the account page. One form, used for both, fixes a whole class of drift.

2. Type is a visible grid, not a dropdown. There are exactly eight types in ACCOUNT_ICONS, each with an icon already defined, and the choice changes which fields appear next. A grid shows the whole set and makes the consequence immediate.

3. Liability sign is explained where it's entered. normalizeLiabilityBalanceForStorage flips the sign so a card balance is stored negative — the user types a positive number meaning "I owe this". Nothing in the form says so, and getting it backwards silently inverts net worth.

4. Day numbers get a preview. statement_day: 16 and due_day: 1 are two bare integers whose relationship — 16 days to pay — is the actually useful fact. daysUntilDayOfMonth already turns them into countdowns everywhere else.

5. All four schedule branches are visible, including the one that's easy to miss. superRefine has four cases, not one: twice a month needs two different entries in loan_due_days; weekly needs loan_due_weekday (0–6, a separate field from the day-of-month one); daily needs neither; everything else needs a single day. Seven periods come from LOAN_PAY_PERIOD_LABELS. Today all of that is discovered on submit — showing which control each period summons is the fix.

6. Available credit computes live. getCreditCardAvailableCredit is credit_limit + balance. Showing it as you type is the cheapest confirmation that the limit and the owed amount were both entered the way you meant.

7. Optional fields say they're optional. credit_limit, statement_day and due_day are all .nullable(), but the form gives no hint that skipping them is allowed — or what you lose, which is the countdowns and the utilisation bar.

What changed, and why

1. Upcoming Bills becomes a strip, not a card. It's first in DEFAULT_WIDGET_ORDER — correctly, since due dates are the most time-sensitive thing on the page — but as a full card it spends a whole grid cell on two rows of text. A single ruled strip keeps the priority and returns the cell.

2. The Credit Card Monitor stops nesting boxes four deep. Card → bordered inner card → four more bordered rows, each its own border-border/40 box, plus up to two coloured reminder strips. At lg:col-span-2 that's the widest widget on the page and the most visually noisy. Two figures share a row instead of stacking, and the reminders collapse to one.

3. The reminder strips use raw Tailwind palette colours. border-amber-500/30 bg-amber-500/5 text-amber-700 and sky-500 / sky-700 are the only two places on Home that reach outside the app's own tokens — everything else uses INCOME, EXPENSE, GOLD from constants/colors. Gold already means "liability due" everywhere else in this audit.

4. Stats cards get comparisons. Same omission as Reports (9a): $3,812.65 with nothing to judge it against. The previous cycle is already loaded.

5. Utilisation colour is binary today. nearLimit ? EXPENSE : INCOME means 0% and 69% are both rendered in the same green, then it snaps to red. A neutral middle band would say more.

6. The forecast's fallback is a literal string. item.tx.category?.icon ?? 'Recur' renders the word "Recur" in an icon-sized slot where every other row shows an emoji. An uncategorised recurring item looks broken.

7. Three columns, not one. Widgets stack in a narrow column today; at 1920 the eight in DEFAULT_WIDGET_ORDER fit in three columns without scrolling, which is what makes a dashboard a dashboard.

8. Mobile shows four widgets, not eight. The user's full order is honoured, but a phone that scrolls through eight cards isn't a glance. Everything below Budget Progress stays available by scrolling — the point is that the first screenful is money, cards and budgets.

What changed, and why

1. The pane says what it belongs to. DetailContent portals into a fixed #dashboard-detail-pane node, so the panel appears at the far right of the window with no visual tie to the widget that opened it. A kicker naming the source widget plus a highlight on that card closes the loop.

2. The close button stops overlapping the title. It's absolute top-2 right-2 over content laid out with p-5 pt-6, and DetailTitle compensates with pr-8 — a manual reservation that only holds while titles stay short. A header row with the button as a sibling removes the class of bug.

3. Escape works in both modes. The keydown listener is gated on pane, so Escape only closes the desktop pane; below lg: it relies on the Dialog. That's correct today but means two different close paths — the mobile sheet also needs an explicit close affordance, which it now has.

4. Widgets get descriptions. The sheet lists bare labels from DASHBOARD_WIDGET_LABELS, so "Category Pie" and "Cash Flow Forecast" are indistinguishable until you enable them and look. One line each turns guessing into choosing.

4b. Two widgets have no switch at all. DashboardWidgets declares ten keys; DEFAULT_WIDGET_ORDER lists eight. The sheet renders widgetOrder.filter((key) => DEFAULT_WIDGET_ORDER.includes(key)), so Savings Goals and Quick Add have persisted toggle state, default to true, and can never be turned off — they're in the data model and unreachable from the UI. Either add them to the order array or drop them from the type.

5. Reorder is one interaction, not two. Desktop gets drag handles (hidden md:block), mobile gets arrow buttons (md:hidden) — two mechanisms, two code paths, and on a touch laptop neither is clearly the right one. Drag with a visible drop indicator works at both sizes; arrows stay as the keyboard-accessible fallback rather than a separate mobile UI.

6. There's a way back to default. useDashboardPrefs exports both DEFAULT_WIDGET_ORDER (an eight-key array) and a DEFAULTS map with every widget true — and nothing in the UI restores either. Hide a few widgets, reorder the rest, and you're reconstructing that order by hand.

7. The trigger isn't portalled into another component's DOM. The sheet does document.getElementById('mobile-dashboard-tools') at render time and portals its own trigger there — a layout dependency that fails silently to an in-place button if that node is missing or renders later. With the header owning a Customise button at every size, the portal goes away.

8. 280px was tight. At 280px a label, drag handle, two arrow buttons and a switch share one row. Dropping the arrows and widening to 320px buys room for the descriptions.

16a

Global search

Doesn't exist yet. cmdk is a dependency and ui/command.tsx exports a full CommandDialog — its only consumer is AccountCombobox, an account picker. The palette is already built and wired to nothing, while the ⌘K affordance in every 2B header assumes it. This is the cheapest large win in the audit.

What changed, and why

1. The dependency gets used. cmdk is installed, ui/command.tsx is 190 lines including a working CommandDialog, and the only thing importing any of it is an account dropdown. The parts are already paid for and shipped to every user's browser.

2. It answers "where is that transaction". A finance app's most common question, and today it needs Activity plus manual cycle-stepping. Searching descriptions, payees, accounts and categories in one field is the whole feature.

3. Numbers search amounts. People remember what something cost more reliably than what it was called. A numeric query matches the exact amount first, then a ±5% band — which is how you find the charge you half-remember as "about eighty-something".

4. The cycle scope is explicit and switchable. Every other screen is bound to the global month cycle from useMonthCycle. Search must either honour it or ignore it, and silently doing either is wrong — so the toggle states which, and the footer offers the other.

5. Commands, not just results. The same letters from 5a — E, I, T — work here, so the palette is a faster Add Transaction than the button. A category query offers "New expense in Groceries", carrying the query into the form.

6. The empty state does work. Before you type: the four record actions, anything due soon from getLoanDeadlines and daysUntilDayOfMonth, and jump-to for all seven destinations — including Categories and Import CSV, which are the two hardest things to reach in the current nav.

7. Mobile gets it as a screen. A centred palette is a desktop pattern; on a phone this is a full-screen view pushed from the header search icon, with the same groups and no keyboard hints.

What changed, and why

1. Two encoding bugs are on screen right now. The subtitle renders "Computed under PD 851 � Select which income records…", the card title "Income Records � 2026", and the transaction meta line uses the same broken byte as a separator. An en dash was written in a non-UTF-8 encoding. Three visible replacement characters on the page, one of them in the first sentence a user reads.

2. The estimate is printed three times. Once in the gold hero band, once in the three-card summary row, once in the table footer — all the same figure with slightly different sub-labels, one of which duplicates the hero's "÷ 12" wording verbatim. Keeping one authoritative statement of it is the single biggest simplification available here.

3. "Auto-select salary only." The whole task is separating basic salary from bonuses and allowances, and the category is already on every record. One button pre-ticking by category turns a 21-row manual pass into a review. The excluded-category chips make the rule visible and reversible.

4. Months start collapsed and stay unreadable. expanded initialises empty, so every month is shut on load and you must click each to see what's inside — while the checkbox that includes or excludes the whole month sits on the same closed row. A flat table with month subtotals shows both levels at once.

5. "Records Included" is coloured with EXPENSE. The third summary card renders a neutral count — 14 / 21 — in the red used everywhere else for money going out. Nothing is wrong; the colour says otherwise.

6. The eligibility rules become a checklist. The PD 851 guidance is a paragraph in an info box that names the exclusions in prose. As a four-row list with tick and cross marks it can be scanned while you're actually ticking rows.

7. Coverage is shown, not just counted. monthsWithIncome of monthsElapsed is a fraction in small text; a twelve-bar strip shows which months are covered, which are partial, and which haven't happened yet — the three states that explain an estimate that looks low.

8. 1920 stops being 768. max-w-3xl caps the page, so the record table — the part you interact with — is squeezed while the summary cards wrap. Table left, results right, and the estimate stays visible while you tick.

9. Say the selection is device-local. It's written to localStorage, so it silently doesn't follow you to another browser or phone. The current copy says "saved locally", which most people read as "saved".

What changed, and why

1. The cost of borrowing gets named. totalPayable is computed and shown; the interest — totalPayable − principal, one subtraction — never is. At 1.25% flat over 24 months that's $720 on a $2,400 purchase, 30% more than the sticker. A form whose entire job is recording a financed purchase should lead with that number.

2. Term and rate stop being on different steps. Step 1 asks the term, step 2 asks the rate — the two inputs that jointly decide the cost, split across a page break, so you can never see the trade-off while adjusting either. At desktop width the whole form fits at once.

3. "Flat interest" is said plainly. It's currently a 12px muted line reading "Estimated using flat monthly interest." Flat versus reducing-balance roughly doubles the effective rate — that deserves a sentence explaining it, not a footnote.

4. Auto-calculation is recoverable. installmentEdited latches true the first time you touch the installment field and never resets, so one stray keystroke permanently disconnects the field from the calculator for the life of the form. A Recalculate affordance costs one line.

5. The schedule is previewed. getPurchaseInstallments already derives every due date via addMonthsClamped, and the final installment is a balancing figure that can differ from the rest. First date, last date and the true final amount are worth three rows.

6. "Already Paid" says what unit it means. The input takes a count of installments; the summary beside it shows "Imported paid" as a currency amount. Two units, adjacent, both unlabelled — 10 of 24 plus the derived amount removes the ambiguity.

7. The effect on the parent loan is shown. This purchase increases what the loan owes and raises the monthly obligation, which is what 5b will later ask you to pay. Neither figure appears in the form today.

8. Rate needs an upper bound. monthly_interest_rate is validated as min(0) with no maximum, so a typo of 125 instead of 1.25 is accepted and silently produces a 31× installment. The live cost panel makes that visible, but the schema should also cap it.

What changed, and why

1. The remainder is one tap, not arithmetic. addLine already seeds the new line with diff — but only if you think to press Add line. Surfacing "$9.40 unassigned → Add as a line" makes the one action that resolves the block visible at the moment it's blocking.

2. Lines become rows, not stacked cards. Each line is a bordered card with description on its own row above category + amount, so three splits run past 400px of height in a max-w-xl dialog. A table row per line fits the same data in a third of the space and lets you compare amounts down a column.

3. A proportion bar. Splitting is inherently about shares of a total; a stacked bar in category colours shows the division and the gap at once, and doubles as the unbalanced indicator.

4. "Over budget" is the wrong phrase. When the lines exceed the original, the dialog says $9.40 over budget — but this has nothing to do with budgets; it's an over-allocation of one transaction. In a product that has a real Budgets screen, that wording sends people to the wrong place.

5. Say that the original is replaced. onConfirm deletes the source transaction and writes N new ones. Nothing in the dialog says so, and it isn't reversible from the UI.

6. Disabled Split says why. The button greys out when unbalanced, when a description is blank, or when any amount is zero — three different causes, one silent state. The balance chip names the one that applies.

What changed, and why

1. It exists. Paying a card is probably the most common liability action in the app, and there is no flow for it — you record a manual expense and hope the balance lands right. TransactionKindMenu has a Loan repayment item and no card equivalent.

2. It is not the loan form with different labels. Loans cap the amount at what's outstanding; cards must not. getAccountAssetBalance explicitly handles a positive card balance as an overpayment, so the model already allows paying more than you owe — the design warns instead of blocking.

3. Utilisation is the number that moves. It's what a card payment is for, getCreditUtilizationPct already computes it, and the before/after bar makes the effect of a partial payment legible in a way a balance figure doesn't.

4. The statement-balance gap is stated, not hidden. Ledger stores one running balance per card and only a statement_day — there is no statement balance. "Pay full balance" therefore clears post-statement purchases too. That's a real modelling limitation; better to say it in the form than let people discover it against a bank statement.

5. Both dates come along. daysUntilDayOfMonth already drives statement and due countdowns on the account card; the payment form is exactly where "closes Sep 16, due Oct 1" decides how much to pay.

6. The category is flagged as excluded from reports. A card payment isn't spending — the spending already happened when the card was used. Counting it again double-counts every expense. Worth being explicit at the point of entry.

7. Recurring is offered here specifically. Card payments are the most repeated transaction most people have, and the due day is already known — so the toggle can prefill the date rather than asking.

What changed, and why

1. The page says what the product does. The one real gap: a stranger landing here sees a wordmark, five words of tagline, and a Google button. There's nothing to sign in for. Three concrete capabilities — multi-account net worth, pay-cycle budgets, bank import — cost one panel and are all true of the app as built.

2. 1920 stops being 400px. max-w-100 centres a phone-width column on a desktop display, so the screen is 80% empty ground. A two-panel split keeps sign-in exactly as narrow as it should be and spends the other half on the case for signing in.

3. Auth errors get a heading and a next step. Today error_description is printed raw — sanitised, correctly, but still raw: "server_error: unable to exchange external code" tells the user nothing. A plain-language title plus "nothing was saved" and a retry beats echoing Supabase.

4. The offline story gets mentioned. AuthContext seeds from cache, there's an offline queue, a receipt store and cache-by-prefix clearing — real PWA work that the login page never alludes to. One install prompt surfaces it.

5. Left-aligned, not centred. The centred stack reads as a splash screen; the content is a form. Ragged-right at 400px is easier to scan and matches every other panel in the app.

6. Two trust lines, near the button. "Google sign-in only — no password to store" and "delete your data any time" are both true (deleteAccount calls the delete_user RPC) and answer the question a finance app has to answer before anyone hands over an account.

7. One logo asset, not two. l-black.png / l-white.png swap on theme, so the mark can't respond to a system theme change without a re-render. A single mark on a fixed tile sidesteps it.

What changed, and why

1. Duplicate detection. The one that matters. Import the same statement twice — or a statement that overlaps last month's by three days — and you get silent duplicates with no way to tell which is which afterwards. Matching on date + amount + normalised description catches this before the write, not after.

2. Category suggestions instead of an apology. category_id: null is hardcoded for every row, and the dialog says so twice — once in a hint box, once in the success screen. A payee-to-category memory from past transactions gets most rows right; the rest show Choose… inline. 142 uncategorized transactions is a chore nobody does later.

3. Rows are selectable. Today it's all-or-nothing: parsed.rows maps straight to the insert. One bad row means cancel, edit the CSV, re-drop. Checkboxes cost nothing and make duplicates actionable rather than just flagged.

4. The preview stops being 8 rows in a 672px dialog. max-w-2xl with PREVIEW_ROW_COUNT = 8 means you approve 142 transactions having seen six percent of them, with +134 more transactions as the only acknowledgement. At 1920 the review is the whole dialog.

5. The account isn't auto-picked. setAccountId(accounts[0].id) selects whatever account happens to be first. Same silent-wrong-target problem as the loan picker in 5b — and here it's 142 rows landing in the wrong account.

6. Currency mismatch is surfaced. The preview formats amounts with selectedAccount?.currency ?? 'PHP' — so a PHP statement imported into a USD account renders as dollars and imports as dollars, with no warning that the numbers are unconverted.

7. Transfers get recognised. ImportTx only allows income | expense, so a transfer between two of your own accounts imports twice — once as an expense, once as income — and inflates both totals. Flagging likely transfers at review is cheaper than reconciling later.

8. The empty state says what the parser expects. Four bank names is all the guidance there is; the requirements (a date column, a description, amount or debit/credit, 5,000 rows) only surface as errors after a failed drop.

What changed, and why

1. Every number gets a comparison. The biggest omission: a reports screen that shows $3,812.65 spent and nothing about whether that's high. The period is already computed, and monthlyData already holds the previous month — so ↑ 11.8% vs Aug costs one subtraction. This is the change I'd make first.

2. Two full-width control cards collapse into the header row. "Date Range" and "Saved Presets" are each a bordered card with an icon, a kicker and a control row — roughly 240px of vertical space spent on chrome before a single figure appears. The presets move behind a button with a count; the range chips move into row two.

3. One set of controls, not two. The date range and presets are built twice — a hidden md:flex card pair for desktop and a separate md:hidden grid of a Select plus a Presets button for mobile. Same state, two markup trees to keep in sync. Chips that scroll horizontally work at all three sizes.

4. Charts stop being 208px tall. Every chart is h-52 regardless of viewport, so a 12-month bar chart gets the same height at 1920 as on a phone. Here the cash-flow chart fills the row it's in, and the y-axis ticks drop to abbreviated 8k/6k instead of formatCurrency strings in a 72px gutter.

5. The transaction table shows all its columns. Six columns are progressively hidden — Category below sm, Account below md, Balance below lg — and max-w-5xl means Balance is hidden at 1024 even though the window is 1920. At full width all seven fit, with a Columns control for anyone who wants fewer.

6. Two different notions of "period" need reconciling. Reports has its own seven presets; the rest of the app runs on the global month cycle from useMonthCycle. 2B's header stepper would contradict the chips here, so Reports is the one screen that suppresses it — worth an explicit decision rather than shipping both.

7. 13th Month is a tab and a route. ThirteenthMonthPage is rendered inside a TabsContent here and registered at /thirteenth-month. Two entry points to one screen, with the tab version nested inside another page's date controls that don't apply to it.

8. Selected chips use the app's own accent. The active preset is styled background: GOLD with --primary-foreground text — the only place in the app where gold means "selected". Gold otherwise means loans.

What changed, and why

1. Categories finally have a nav entry. /categories exists as a route with no desktop or tablet destination — you can only reach it from the mobile More sheet. 2B's tab row is the fix, and this is the screen that proves it.

2. Rows carry usage. Today a row is emoji, name, type badge — nothing about whether the category is used. Spend this cycle, share of spending, transaction count and subcategory count are all things the page already has access to, and they're what you need to decide whether a category should exist.

3. Subcategories move to a detail pane. expandedCategoryId is a single value, so exactly one category can be open and you can never compare two. A pane also gives the subcategory list room for per-subcategory spend instead of a bare name and two icon buttons.

4. Auto-categorization comes out of the … menu. It's a real feature — keyword, category, type hint, priority — hidden behind an unlabelled MoreHorizontal button, in a dialog whose form is five controls in a flex-wrap. Here it's a labelled button with a rule count, and each category's own rules show in its pane.

5. Reorder becomes one visible control. rearrangeMode currently ships two implementations — HTML5 drag above 768px, Up/Down arrow buttons below — plus a media-query listener to switch between them, all entered from a hidden menu item.

6. An "Unused" tab, and Merge. Unused surfaces the 3 categories with no transactions — the ones safe to delete. Merge is the action people actually want when they have Dining and Restaurants; without it the only option is delete, which uncategorizes every transaction that used it.

7. Delete should say what it costs. The confirmation reads "Transactions using it will become uncategorized" without a number. The pane shows 38 transactions, so the dialog can say 38.

8. both-type categories are marked. A category of type both is rendered into the Expenses and Income tab by two separate filters, so the same row appears twice with no indication it's one record. Salary is labelled "Income & Expense" and its spend column says which side you're looking at.

What changed, and why

1. The rail selects a pane instead of scrolling to one. This deletes the entire scroll-spy: getScrollParent, spyLockRef, the 150ms settle timer, the 1200ms fallback, the "trailing sections can't reach the line" special case — roughly 100 lines of state whose only job is guessing which heading you're looking at. A pane always knows.

2. Content stops being capped at 640px. max-w-5xl plus lg:max-w-[640px] means a 1920 display shows a 640px column of forms. One pane at a time can afford a preview beside it.

3. Tablet labels go from 9.5px to 13px. max-lg:text-[9.5px] under a 44px icon is the smallest type in the app by a wide margin. Horizontal sub-tabs carry full labels at a legible size.

4. Eight flat sections become three groups. You / How Ledger works / Account. Profile, Appearance and Notifications are about you; formats, cycle and rates are about the app's behaviour; sign-out and delete are neither and shouldn't sit in the same scroll as your display name.

5. Text size becomes a slider with one live preview. Today it's four buttons each rendering its own label at its own size — so "Small" is 12px, below the app's minimum, and you judge the setting from four inconsistent samples instead of seeing the result.

6. Current values surface in the rail and the mobile index. Month cycle · 1st, Light · Medium text, and a count badge when a currency is missing a rate — so you can answer "what is this set to?" without opening the pane. The missing-rate badge also connects to the excluded-currency warning in 6a.

7. System theme joins Light and Dark. ThemeContext only stores the two, so the app can't follow the OS — the one appearance setting most users never touch again once it's right.

What changed, and why

1. The page stops being 1024px wide. max-w-5xl caps this screen no matter the display; at 1920 that's 900px of empty gutter. Assets and Liabilities now sit side by side, which is also the comparison the page is actually about.

2. Assets rows carry a share bar. Today a row is name, type, balance — six numbers you have to divide in your head. The share column answers "how concentrated am I?" at a glance.

3. The excluded-currency warning moves onto the row. It's currently one amber line under the summary band naming currencies, so you can't tell which account was left out of the total. Now the row says so, and the footnote just links to Settings.

4. Due dates get one home. "Due in Nd" chips are scattered across liability cards; the band's Coming-up cell collects them with amounts, so the next payment is visible without reading every card.

5. Liability cards get their action. Each card is a single <button> that navigates today. Pay card / Repay loan wire straight into 5b — the thing you came here to do.

6. Loan progress becomes a meter. Cards show a utilisation bar; loans show only a schedule string. 34 of 48 paid is the same kind of fact and deserves the same bar.

Full-width rows, 64px targets, descriptions on one line, and the reachable end of the screen. Same five items, same order, same strings.

On mobile

A dropdown is the wrong pattern here. TransactionKindMenu is a Radix DropdownMenu with w-72, and on mobile its trigger is the FAB in the bottom-right corner — so the menu renders as a 288px panel pinned to that corner, overlapping the bottom nav, with every description wrapping to two lines. It's the same component doing desktop duty on a phone.

The app already owns the alternative. ui/sheet.tsx ships and the mobile More nav item already opens as a bottom sheet — so this is a trigger swap below md, not a new component. Keep the dropdown on desktop where a FAB isn't involved.

Targets go from 56px to 64px and gain the full 390px width, which matters for the one control standing in front of every entry in the app.

Keyboard letters are dropped, not hidden. E / I / T earn their place on desktop; on mobile they're noise in a row that's already carrying a description and an amount.

Three changes, all cheap: a Liabilities group so repayment reads as a different class of action rather than an afterthought below a divider; the amount owed on the item, since that's the number you're about to act on; and keyboard letters, because this menu is the one gate in front of every entry.

Card payment is the same shape as loan repayment — an expense that lands against a liability — and today it has no entry point here at all. Say the word and I'll leave it out.

Kind is asked once, not twice

The duplication. TransactionKindMenu makes you choose Expense / Income / Transfer / Loan repayment before the modal opens — then TransactionForm renders a three-way type selector as the first control inside it, pre-set to what you just picked. The same decision, asked twice, two seconds apart.

Creating: the kind becomes the modal's identity — tinted icon, "New expense" as the title, the menu's own description as the subtitle. It reads as confirmation of what you chose rather than a question you've already answered.

Editing: the selector belongs here, because the kind is now a property of a saved record rather than a choice being made. It's the only route to fixing a mis-typed entry — today you'd delete and re-record.

One thing to keep. A mis-pick in the menu currently costs Cancel plus a reopen, so the create header keeps a Change kind link back to the menu. Without it, removing the selector trades a redundancy for a dead end.

Loan repayment and card payment are unaffected. Both already lock the type — disabled={isLoanRepayment} — so they render a disabled control that can never change. See 5b and 12a, where the kind is stated in the title and no selector appears at all.
